A Bootstrap modal is a dozen nested divs with the right classes, the right `data-bs-` attributes, and the right ARIA wiring.
Writing that by hand in a Quarto document means writing raw HTML, and losing markdown inside it.

`modal` writes the wiring for you.
A div whose identifier starts with `modal-` becomes the dialog, its first heading becomes the title, and a shortcode gives you the button that opens it.
The content stays markdown throughout.

## Installation

```bash
quarto add {{< var extension.reference >}}
```

This will install the extension under the `_extensions` subdirectory.
If you are using version control, you will want to check in this directory.

Or install it from your editor with [Quarto Wizard](https://m.canouil.dev/quarto-wizard):

::: {.btn-group role="group" aria-label="Quarto Wizard installer options"}

## Quick start

Enable the filter:

```yaml
filters:
  - path: modal
    at: pre-quarto
```

Then write the container and a button that opens it:

```markdown
{{{< modal toggle target=modal-hello label="Say hello" >}}}

::: {#modal-hello}
## Hello

The body of the modal, written as ordinary markdown.
:::
```

Which gives you this:

{{< modal toggle target=modal-hello label="Say hello" >}}

::: {#modal-hello}
## Hello

The body of the modal, written as ordinary markdown.
:::

The identifier has to start with `modal-`; that prefix is how the extension tells a dialog from any other div.

See the [Reference](reference.qmd) for every option, and the [Examples](examples.qmd) for each of them rendered.

## Where it works

HTML formats that carry JavaScript **and** Bootstrap, which is Quarto's default `html` and its website and book projects.

::: {.callout-note}
Where Bootstrap is absent, `revealjs` among others, the filter leaves the document alone: the container renders as an ordinary div and the button as ordinary text.
Nothing breaks, and nothing pops up.
:::
